title: General Truncation Divisibility Rule
description: A parametric theorem generalizing the truncation method to all divisors coprime to 10. Given any d coprime to 10 and an osculator c (satisfying d | 10c ∓ 1), we prove d | n ↔ d | (n/10 ± c·(n%10)). This single theorem subsumes the specific rules for 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37, and all other primes coprime to 10.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules have been studied since antiquity. The rules for 3 and 9 (sum of digits), 11 (alternating sum), 7 and 13 (truncation methods) are classical results. The **truncation method** or **osculator method** is attributed to various 19th-century mathematicians including Kummer (1852) and Zuckerman (1948). The key insight is that for any integer $d$ coprime to 10, there exists a multiplicative inverse of 10 mod $d$, the **osculator**, connecting $d$-divisibility of $n$ to a simpler expression in $\lfloor n/10 \rfloor$ and $n \bmod 10$. This single algebraic principle unifies dozens of seemingly ad-hoc pencil-and-paper tests into one parametric theorem, formalized in Lean 4 with `IsCoprime` and `linear_combination`.
overview.problemStatement:
Can the individual truncation rules for 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 be unified into a single parametric theorem?

Specifically: given d coprime to 10, is there a general rule of the form $d | n \iff d | f(n/10, n\%10)$ where $f$ depends only on $d$?

**Answer: YES**, with two variants:
- **Positive osculator** ($d | 10c - 1$): $d | n \iff d | (n/10 + c \cdot (n\%10))$
- **Negative osculator** ($d | 10c + 1$): $d | n \iff d | (n/10 - c \cdot (n\%10))$
overview.text: A parametric theorem generalizing the truncation method to all divisors coprime to 10. Given any d coprime to 10 and an osculator c (satisfying d | 10c ∓ 1), we prove d | n ↔ d | (n/10 ± c·(n%10)). This single theorem subsumes the specific rules for 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, 31, 37, and all other primes coprime to 10.
overview.proofStrategy:
The key algebraic identity is:
$$10 \cdot (n/10 + c \cdot (n\%10)) = n + (10c - 1) \cdot (n\%10)$$

When $d | (10c - 1)$, the term $(10c-1) \cdot (n\%10)$ is divisible by $d$, so:
$$d | n \iff d | n + (10c-1)(n\%10) = 10 \cdot (n/10 + c \cdot (n\%10))$$

Since $\gcd(d, 10) = 1$, divisibility by $d$ transfers through the factor 10:
$$d | 10 \cdot \text{expr} \iff d | \text{expr}$$

Formally: `IsCoprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` handles this last step.

The negative osculator case is symmetric, with the identity:
$$10 \cdot (n/10 - c \cdot (n\%10)) = n - (10c + 1) \cdot (n\%10)$$
keyInsights: The `linear_combination` tactic elegantly handles the algebraic identity: `linear_combination -hdiv` where `hdiv : n = 10*(n/10) + n%10`.
The `IsCoprime` condition in Lean 4 provides exactly the right algebraic framework: coprimeness lets us cancel the factor of 10.
The positive osculator c satisfies 10c ≡ 1 (mod d), i.e., c is the multiplicative inverse of 10 mod d.
The negative osculator satisfies 10c ≡ -1 (mod d), i.e., c is the 'negative inverse' of 10 mod d.
Every d coprime to 10 has both positive and negative osculators (they are multiplicative inverses of 10 and -10 respectively).
The proof works uniformly for all d, not just primes.
prerequisites: Modular arithmetic and coprimality ($\gcd(d, 10) = 1$, multiplicative inverses in $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$)
Division algorithm: $n = 10 \cdot \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10)$ for digit extraction
Bézout's identity and `IsCoprime` (cancelling a coprime factor from a divisibility relation)
Elementary divisibility theory (transitivity, linearity of divisibility over sums)

conclusion.summary: The truncation method generalizes to a complete parametric framework. Two theorems (`truncation_pos` and `truncation_neg`) cover all cases: for any d coprime to 10, there exist osculator constants c (the multiplicative inverse of ±10 mod d) giving divisibility tests. The proof uses a single algebraic identity and the `IsCoprime` machinery of Mathlib.
conclusion.implications:
This unification has both mathematical and pedagogical value:
- **Mathematical**: Shows the truncation method is not a collection of ad-hoc tricks but a single algebraic phenomenon.
- **Computational**: Given any d coprime to 10, one can immediately compute the osculator and generate a divisibility test.
- **Formal verification**: The parametric theorem is easier to maintain and extend than individual proofs.

The framework also extends to multi-digit truncation (the OQ-02 extension) and to arbitrary bases.
openQuestions: ANSWERED (see divisibility-truncation-general-oq-01): The positive and negative osculator theorems merge into a single unified_osculator theorem. The negative case is the positive case with c negated.
Can this be extended to divisors that share factors with 10 (i.e., d = 2, 5, 4, 8, 25, etc.) by combining with the last-k-digits framework?
What is the relationship between the osculator and the continued fraction expansion of 1/d?
